sections.skill: Use loan payments to find total cost, and compare loan terms

questions.prompt: A $12,000 car loan at 6% APR for 5 years has a monthly payment of $231.99. What is the total of all payments?
questions.intro: An installment loan is repaid in equal scheduled payments, such as monthly car or personal loan payments. Total paid = payment × number of payments. Total interest = total paid − amount borrowed.
questions.topic: Installment loans: payments and total cost
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: $15,000 at 7% APR: a 36-month loan has payments of $463.16; a 72-month loan has payments of $255.74. How much MORE interest does the 72-month loan cost?
questions.intro: A longer term lowers the monthly payment but usually raises the total interest, because the balance is outstanding longer.

questions.prompt: A 72-month car loan costs more total interest than a 36-month loan for the same amount. Why might someone choose the 72-month loan anyway?

choices.text: It always has a lower total cost because payments are smaller
It pays off the car sooner
Its lower monthly payment fits a tight budget

questions.correct_answer: Its lower monthly payment fits a tight budget
questions.feedback: The trade-off: lower payments now, more total interest.

questions.prompt: The monthly payment on a loan is M = P · r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^(−n)), where r is the monthly rate and n is the number of payments. For $10,000 at 6% APR for 60 months, what is r?
questions.intro: The standard loan payment formula uses the monthly rate r = APR ÷ 12 (as a decimal) and the number of monthly payments n.
questions.topic: Installment loans: payments and total cost

misconceptions.D: Uses the percent as a decimal

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Using M = P · r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^(−n)) with P = $10,000, r = 0.005, and n = 60, what is the monthly payment (nearest cent)?
questions.intro: Evaluate the formula with a calculator: compute (1 + r)^(−n) first, then the denominator, then multiply P by r and divide.
questions.topic: Installment loans: payments and total cost

misconceptions.D: Adds simple interest for one year to each payment

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: $5,000 at 10% APR for 24 months: the payment is $230.72. If the APR were 0%, what would the payment be (nearest cent)?
questions.intro: With no interest, payments simply divide the principal evenly: P ÷ n.
questions.topic: Installment loans: payments and total cost
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: A loan payment calculator shows $405.53 for $20,000 at 8% APR over 60 months. Which check shows the result is reasonable?

choices.text: It is a bit more than $20,000 ÷ 60 = $333.33

questions.correct_answer: It is a bit more than $20,000 ÷ 60 = $333.33
questions.intro: A quick check: a loan payment must be more than the principal divided by the number of payments, because interest is added.
questions.feedback: $405.53 > $333.33, as expected when interest is charged.
questions.topic: Installment loans: payments and total cost

misconceptions.B: Payments cannot be below principal ÷ months
misconceptions.C: Confuses with one year of interest

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Before visiting a car dealer, Rosa gets a preapproved loan offer from her credit union. Why is this useful?

choices.text: She can compare it with the dealer's financing offer
It guarantees the lowest possible rate at every dealer anywhere
It removes the need to read the contract

questions.correct_answer: She can compare it with the dealer's financing offer
questions.intro: Getting a loan offer from a bank or credit union before shopping gives you a benchmark. If the dealer offers a better rate, you can take it; if not, you have an alternative.
questions.feedback: A preapproval gives her a rate to compare against the dealer's offer.
questions.topic: Installment loans: payments and total cost

misconceptions.B: Preapproval does not set the price

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: A dealer says, "What monthly payment do you want?" What risk does focusing on the payment create?

choices.text: The APR must drop by law when the loan term gets longer
The term can be stretched, raising total interest

questions.correct_answer: The term can be stretched, raising total interest
questions.intro: Any monthly payment can be reached by stretching the term, which hides the extra interest. Negotiate the price first, then compare financing by APR and total cost.
questions.feedback: Lower payments from a longer term can cost much more in total.
questions.topic: Installment loans: payments and total cost
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Offer 1: 4.9% APR for 48 months, payment $230. Offer 2: 6.9% APR for 60 months, payment $198. Which costs less in total?

choices.text: Offer 2, because its payment is lower

questions.intro: To compare offers with different terms, compute each total of payments: payment × number of payments.
questions.topic: Installment loans: payments and total cost
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which loan feature lets a borrower pay off early without a penalty?

choices.text: An extended warranty on the car

questions.intro: Some loans charge a fee for paying them off early (a prepayment penalty). Choosing a loan without one lets you save interest by paying it down faster.
questions.feedback: Without a prepayment penalty, extra payments save interest at no cost.
questions.topic: Installment loans: payments and total cost
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: A loan has a "balloon payment." What does that mean?

choices.text: A large lump sum is due at the end
Payments get smaller and smaller each month

questions.correct_answer: A large lump sum is due at the end
questions.intro: A balloon loan has small regular payments followed by a very large final payment. Borrowers who cannot pay the balloon may need to refinance or sell.
questions.feedback: A balloon is a big final payment that must be planned for.
questions.topic: Installment loans: payments and total cost
